::: {.callout-note}
## Attribution

The π example and the order of the cases come from George G. Vega Yon's workshop *HPC with Slurm, R and the slurmR package* (<https://github.com/USCbiostats/slurmr-workshop>{target="_blank"}). I adapted it to CHPC and replaced the slurmR functions with plain Slurm. The Codex setup follows CHPC's session *Coding Agents at CHPC* from November 10.
:::

## Learning goals

By the end of this lab you should be able to:

- run the same simulation serially, on several cores, and as a job array, and get the same result each time;
- request cores from Slurm and have R use exactly those;
- split a simulation across array tasks and combine the results with a second, dependent job;
- use Codex on CHPC to write and debug Slurm jobs, and check its work;
- measure the speedup you get and explain why it's below the number of cores.

## How this lab works

Work in pairs. You each need your own CHPC account, but feel free to share a screen. As in the other labs, keep a log of the prompts you send to Codex, with a line or two on what came back. The log is part of what you hand in.

Put everything in a new folder `lab11/` in your class repository: `lab11.qmd`, the rendered HTML, your scripts, and `timings.csv`. It's due Sunday, as usual.

| When | What | Time |
|---|---|---|
| Before class | [Checklist](#before-class) | 10 min |
| In class | [Hands-on 1](#hands-on-1): cases 1 and 2 by hand | 20 min |
| In class | [Hands-on 2](#hands-on-2): Codex writes the job array | 35 min |
| At home | [Homework](#homework): buggy script, scaling report | 50 min |

You'll need these numbers throughout. A correct version of the simulation prints exactly these values:

| `nsims`, `n` | Used for | π̂ |
|---|---|---|
| 100, 10,000 | small tests | 3.140208000000 |
| 10,000, 10,000 (default) | quick runs and the buggy script | 3.141755000000 |
| 10,000, 100,000 | timing runs | 3.141601060000 |

## Before class (10 minutes) {#before-class}

1. Log in to [Open OnDemand](https://ondemand.chpc.utah.edu){target="_blank"} and start an interactive desktop session. (Codex needs a browser on the same machine to sign you in, which is why we use the desktop and not a plain ssh session.) Open a terminal in the desktop and copy the scripts:

    ```bash
    git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/UofUEpiBio/PHS7045-advanced-programming.git ~/phs7045-course
    mkdir -p ~/lab11
    cp -r ~/phs7045-course/11-simpi/scripts/. ~/lab11/
    cd ~/lab11 && ls
    ```

    You should see `simpi.R`, a few `.R` and `.slurm` files, `AGENTS.md`, and a folder called `buggy/`.

2. Start Codex and sign in:

    ```bash
    module load codex
    cd ~/lab11
    codex
    ```

    A browser window opens; sign in with your university account. To check that Codex picked up the lab rules, ask it *"Which rules apply in this folder?"* It should describe what's in `AGENTS.md`. Then exit.

3. If signing in doesn't work, try `module load codex_CHPC_local_model`, which uses a model hosted at CHPC and doesn't need a login. Let us know at the start of class.

4. On your laptop, make the `lab11/` folder in your class repository, put the same scripts in it (copy them from the course repository, or use `scp -r <uid>@notchpeak.chpc.utah.edu:~/lab11/ .`), and create `lab11.qmd`.

## Hands-on 1: cases 1 and 2 by hand (20 minutes) {#hands-on-1}

Please do this part without Codex. These are the steps you'll repeat every time you use the cluster, so it's worth typing them yourself once.

### 1a. On your laptop (8 minutes)

From the `lab11/` folder on your laptop:

```bash
Rscript 01-sapply.R                       # default size
Rscript 01-sapply.R 10000 100000          # timing size, about 30 s
Rscript 02-mclapply.R 10000 100000 4      # same, on 4 cores
```

On Windows, `02-mclapply.R` uses a socket cluster instead of `mclapply()`; you don't have to change anything.

Create a file `timings.csv` like the one below and fill in the first two rows with the elapsed time and π̂ from the output:

```default
where,tasks,cores_per_task,total_cores,elapsed_sec,pi_hat
laptop,1,1,1,,
laptop,1,4,4,,
chpc,1,4,4,,
chpc,4,4,16,,
```

Questions for `lab11.qmd`:

a. Does the default run print the known answer? Do both timing runs print the same π̂?

b. What speedup $S_4 = T_1 / T_4$ did you get, and why isn't it 4?

### 1b. On CHPC (12 minutes)

In the OnDemand terminal, inside `~/lab11`:

```bash
cat 00-hello-world.slurm          # read it first
sbatch 00-hello-world.slurm
squeue --me                       # PD = waiting, R = running
cat hello-world-*.out             # once it has finished
```

Next, read `02-mclapply.slurm` and `02-mclapply.R` and submit the job. You don't need to wait for it; it runs on its own while you continue.

```bash
sbatch 02-mclapply.slurm          # note the job ID
```

Once it has finished, look at the log (`02-mclapply-<jobid>.out`) and save the accounting information. You'll need it for the homework:

```bash
sacct -j <jobid> --format=JobID,JobName,Start,End,Elapsed,AllocCPUS,TotalCPU,NodeList,State --parsable2 > sacct-02-mclapply.txt
```

Questions for `lab11.qmd`:

c. Which node ran your hello-world job? Was it a login node?

d. How does `02-mclapply.R` know how many cores it can use? What could go wrong if it used `parallel::detectCores()` instead?

e. Did you get the same π̂ on CHPC as on your laptop?

## Hands-on 2: Codex writes the job array (35 minutes) {#hands-on-2}

Now the simulation runs as a job array with 4 tasks and 4 cores per task, plus one more job that combines the results. Codex writes the scripts; you decide what they need to do, test them, and submit them.

### 2a. Write down what you expect (5 minutes)

Before you open Codex, copy this into `lab11.qmd` and fill in the blanks:

```default
Goal: run the pi simulation (nsims = 10000, n = 100000) as a Slurm job array
with 4 tasks and 4 cores per task, reusing simpi.R, and combine the results
in a second job.

Acceptance tests (and how I will check each one):
1. The combined pi-hat is ______________ to all 12 digits.
   Check: ____________________________________________
2. Every task records the node it ran on.
   Check: ____________________________________________
3. Every task writes its own file; after the run there are exactly ___ files.
   Check: ____________________________________________
4. The combining job starts only after all tasks finished successfully.
   Check: ____________________________________________
```

### 2b. Ask for a plan, then the code (15 minutes)

Start Codex in `~/lab11` (`module load codex`, then `codex`) and paste the prompt below, with your four tests in place of the bracketed line:

```{.default}
P1
Read @simpi.R, @02-mclapply.R, @02-mclapply.slurm and AGENTS.md.
I want to run the same pi simulation (nsims = 10000, n = 100000) as a Slurm
job array with 4 tasks and 4 cores per task, plus a second job that combines
the results. My acceptance tests are:
[paste your four tests here]
Do not write any files yet. Propose a plan: which files you will create, how
the replicates are split across tasks, what each task saves, and the exact
commands I should run to test it on a tiny problem and to submit it.
```

Read the plan carefully. Does it use `make_seeds()` and `simpi()` as they are? Does each task save to a separate file? If not, ask Codex to change the plan. Once you're happy with it:

```{.default}
P2
The plan looks good. Write 03-array.R, 03-array.slurm, 04-aggregate.R and
04-aggregate.slurm. Use the same account and partition as 02-mclapply.slurm.
```

### 2c. Test small, then submit (10 minutes)

Before submitting anything, run a small version on the login node. Our `AGENTS.md` allows this for small sizes. Since there's no Slurm here, you set the array variables yourself:

```bash
for a in 1 2 3 4; do
  SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID=$a SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_COUNT=4 SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK=1 \
    Rscript 03-array.R 100 10000
done
Rscript 04-aggregate.R 100 10000     # should print 3.140208000000
bash -n 03-array.slurm && bash -n 04-aggregate.slurm && echo "syntax OK"
```

Codex's scripts may take the size differently; if so, adjust the commands. When the small test works, move its output out of the way (`mv results results-tiny`) and submit the real thing yourself:

```bash
jid=$(sbatch --parsable 03-array.slurm)
echo "array job ID: $jid"        # write it down; you need it for sacct
sbatch --dependency=afterok:$jid 04-aggregate.slurm
squeue --me
```

### 2d. Check (5 minutes)

When both jobs have finished, go through your four tests and note which ones passed. Then save the accounting information for the array:

```bash
sacct -j <array job ID> --format=JobID,JobName,Start,End,Elapsed,AllocCPUS,TotalCPU,NodeList,State --parsable2 > sacct-03-array.txt
```

Questions for `lab11.qmd`:

f. Which tests passed the first time? What did you have to fix, and would you have noticed the problem without the known answer?

g. How many different nodes did your 4 tasks run on? Why could they all end up on the same one?

## Homework (about 50 minutes) {#homework}

### H1. A buggy script (15 minutes)

The `buggy/` folder contains a classmate's version of case 2, `05-buggy.R` and `05-buggy.slurm`. There are three problems in it.

a. Read both files, without running anything, and write down every problem you can find. Give yourself about 5 minutes.

b. Submit it: `cd ~/lab11/buggy && sbatch 05-buggy.slurm`. What happens?

c. Ask Codex. CHPC's `job-triage` skill should be used here.

    ```{.default}
    P3
    My job script @buggy/05-buggy.slurm does not run, and I suspect that
    @buggy/05-buggy.R has problems too. Diagnose both files. Do not change
    anything yet: list each problem, how you found it, and how to fix it.
    ```

d. Fix only the problem in the Slurm script and submit again. Compare π̂ with the known answer for this size (3.141755000000). Then submit it once more. Do you get the same number twice?

e. Fill in this table in `lab11.qmd`:

    | Problem | Did I find it? | Did Codex find it? | How did it show up? (error / wrong answer / not at all) |
    |---|---|---|---|
    | | | | |
    | | | | |
    | | | | |

    Which of these would you have missed if you hadn't known the right answer?

### H2. Scaling report (30 minutes)

Fill in the two CHPC rows of `timings.csv` using `sacct-02-mclapply.txt` and `sacct-03-array.txt`. For the array, count the time from when the first task started to when the last one finished. You can ask Codex to help:

```{.default}
P4
Read @sacct-02-mclapply.txt and @sacct-03-array.txt. For each job, report
the wall time (for the array: from the first task's start to the last task's
end), the allocated cores, and the CPU efficiency (TotalCPU divided by
Elapsed x AllocCPUS). Then write an R script scaling.R that reads
@timings.csv, adds speedup (relative to the laptop with 1 core) and
efficiency columns, and plots speedup against total cores with a dashed
line for perfect scaling.
```

Then:

a. Choose one row and work out its wall time and efficiency yourself from the `sacct` file. Do you agree with Codex?

b. Add the table and the plot to `lab11.qmd` by running `scaling.R` in a chunk.

c. Answer briefly:

    1. Why is the speedup on 16 cores lower than 16? Point to at least two reasons you can see in your own numbers.
    2. Imagine each replicate took a hundredth of a second and you split the work into 1,000 array tasks. What would take most of the time?
    3. Think about the simulation for your final project. How would you set it up in the same way, with replicates, one seed per replicate, and one output file per task?

### H3. Hand it in (5 minutes)

Copy your files from CHPC to your laptop (`scp -r <uid>@notchpeak.chpc.utah.edu:~/lab11/ .`) and push the `lab11/` folder of your class repository. It should contain:

- `lab11.qmd` and the rendered HTML, with your prompt log (P1 to P4 and any follow-up prompts, each with a short note on what came back);
- your filled-in acceptance tests, each marked as passed or failed;
- the `03-array.*` and `04-aggregate.*` scripts (including your fixes) and your corrected `05-buggy.*`;
- `timings.csv`, the `sacct-*.txt` files, and `scaling.R`.
